Recommend correcting on the verdict re-propose for completeness.

This dual-role pattern (risk_analyst produces both a standalone risk register and a verdict-on-others) is acceptable — the risk register itself is what I'm reviewing here, and it stands on its own. body:
Reviewed both architect artifacts (2817-architect-output.json, 399 lines; 2817-architect-slices.yaml, 27 slices). The plan addresses ALL 5 risk_analyst blocking concerns concretely:

### blocker-1 (per-phase _run_pipeline carve-out) — ADDRESSED
slice-7 explicitly mandates the two-stage refactor: (1) PHASE_HANDLERS dispatch table introduction; (2) lift each phase body into _run_loop/_run_refine.py / _run_plan.py / _run_implement.py / _run_pr.py + thin _run_loop/_orchestration.py (<300 LOC). Acceptance includes manual smoke-run + #2319 follow-up. td-2 and td-7 carry contingency for 2-slice sub-split if convergence stalls. The new functions don't exist today — confirmed in my own grep (`grep '^def _run_(refine|plan|pr)_phase'` returns zero hits) — so the slice text correctly frames it as fresh extraction.

### blocker-2 (allowlist serialization protocol) — ADDRESSED
Three load-bearing mechanisms: (a) td-3 keeps intermediate sub-slice allowlist entries intact (only terminal sub-slice removes), shrinking the YAML conflict surface to terminal-only commits; (b) chained sub-slices serialize barrel mutation for outliers (no parallel rebase storms inside pipelines.py / gateway.py); (c) primitive_citations.allowlist_rebase_recipe + r-10 reference docs/guides/decomposition-pattern.md:186-214 for the documented rebase choreography. Parallel sibling slices (slice-13..slice-27) still mutate the allowlist concurrently under EGG_ORCH_MAX_PARALLEL_SLICES=2, but the surface is bounded — each only drops its own entry.

### blocker-3 (plan_parser.py in scope) — ADDRESSED
slice-24 is "shared/egg_contracts/plan_parser.py decomposition" with full submodule scaffold (_models / _yaml / _markdown / _top / _forest / _role_alignment / _preflight). background.operator_hitl_resolutions.cq-3 explicitly notes "#2569 closed by operator; shared/egg_contracts/plan_parser.py is IN SCOPE of this pipeline." cq-5 retag for plan_parser.py allowlist comment from #2548 → #2817 lands in slice-1; the entry itself comes out in slice-24.

### blocker-4 (lazy-import audit for routes.pipelines symbols) — ADDRESSED
Three explicit references: (a) primitive_citations.phases_py_lazy_imports constraint ("submodules carved out of phases.py MUST preserve the lazy in-function imports, not hoist them to module-level — hoisting reintroduces the cycle"); (b) td-6 ("phases.py decomposition preserves lazy in-function imports"); (c) slice-26 ("CRITICAL: preserve lazy in-function imports... hoisting to module-level reintroduces the import cycle with pipelines.py"). r-6 catches the regression vector. Note: the architect's r-3 mentions the audit recipe but doesn't explicitly mandate un-anchored grep for in-function imports across all importers (not just phases.py) — see Non-blocking #3 below.

### blocker-5 (gateway.py @app.route decorators stay in __init__.py) — ADDRESSED
Four references reinforce HITL decision-8: (a) primitive_citations.routes_handling_convention; (b) cluster_scaffold_recommendations["gateway/gateway.py"].note; (c) slice-8: "Routes still register via @app.route(...) thin wrappers in __init__.py (HITL decision-8 of #2261)"; (d) the routes_stay_in_init list under pipelines.py scaffold also documents the equivalent @<bp>.route convention for orchestrator routes.

### Strengths
- **27-slice structure directly addresses the prior-failure mode (RISK-1).** The six-cycle history of #2261-v3..v10 stalled because slices were too large; the chained sub-slices (pipelines.py 6 → gateway.py 5) cap each PR at one BRC cycle's worth of work. r-11 acknowledges this risk explicitly.
- **Forest constraint verified.** Every slice has ≤1 parent: slice-1 is root, slice-2..7 form the pipelines.py chain, slice-8..12 the gateway.py chain, slice-13..27 all parent on slice-1. No multi-parent violations; slice-DAG runtime accepts.
- **Up-front docs slice (slice-1) consolidates cq-2 + cq-4 + cq-5 + cq-6 work into one reviewable PR.** This is the right packaging — these have no natural per-file owner among the decomposition slices, and inlining would scatter them across 15+ PRs with arbitrary first-touch ordering.
- **HARD slices (monitor.py / peer_consensus.py / phases.py / git_push) are flagged with contingencies** (td-5, td-7, r-7, r-8). Reviewer_plan NACK-on-slice_size mechanism is the safety net.
- **Cluster scaffolds at the right resolution.** Named as GUIDANCE per td-4, not prescription; implementing agent owns final cluster boundaries. Reduces architect rework when an implementing agent finds a better seam.

### Non-blocking
- **Sub-sub-package barrels (slice-3/4/5/6) add a double-hop re-export layer.** Each cluster's _<name>/__init__.py barrel re-exports symbols; the parent pipelines/__init__.py also re-exports the cluster module's surface. Both barrels must be audited per slice. Pattern doc §(d) audit recipe handles single-layer; for nested layers, the audit must traverse both — minor risk worth noting in implementer task lists.
- **Slice-2 TBD placeholders for the 5 sub-sub-packages must be valid Python.** If `_prompt_building/` is reserved as a comment-only placeholder in __init__.py (e.g. `# TBD: _prompt_building/ in slice-3`), the placeholder must not import a non-existent module. Implementing agent for slice-2 should verify the placeholder shape doesn't break collection.
- **r-3 (barrel-regression) mitigation references the audit recipe but doesn't explicitly call out in-function lazy imports across ALL importers (not just phases.py).** The blocker-4 finding catches this for phases.py + mcp_tools.py (the two I verified at lines 405/535/612/711/733/1010/1189/1307 and 1609/1680 respectively); the implementer for any pipelines.py sub-slice should run `git grep 'from routes.pipelines'` un-anchored across the whole repo to catch additional in-function importers I may have missed. Worth adding a one-line note in slice-2's task description.
- **mcp_tools.py lazy imports use the DOUBLE-prefix form** `from orchestrator.routes.pipelines import _read_phase_draft / _pipeline_identifier`, not the single-prefix form (correcting my own risk register's RISK-4 evidence). Substantive point holds either way: un-anchored grep catches both shapes; barrel must re-export both symbols. The architect's audit recipe and slice-15 (mcp_tools.py decomposition) don't need to change — the existing slice scaffold is correct.
- **Concurrency caps**: BRC state shows slice_admit.cap=4 globally; architect cites EGG_ORCH_MAX_PARALLEL_SLICES=2 per-pipeline + EGG_ORCH_GLOBAL_MAX_PARALLEL_SLICES=4 process-wide. Both correct — the per-pipeline cap is the binding constraint for this pipeline's wave structure. r-1 acknowledges; the operator can lower to 1 if scheduler pressure surfaces.
- **gateway.py git_push helpers may cross the cap** (slice-9 note). The "further-split" escape hatch in pattern doc §(g) is correct, but if git_push helpers exceed 1500 LOC on first extraction, slice-9 itself may need a 2-sub-slice split before merging. r-5 and security_review ACK requirement catch this; worth flagging that slice-9 carries the highest single-slice complexity in the gateway.py chain.

The plan is concrete, evidence-grounded, forest-valid, and conservatively sized for the failure-mode history. ACK from risk lens.

**Adversarial re-review**

**Your v2 review has TWO equal-weight mandates:**

1. **Verify named v1 blockers were addressed** — confirm the producer fixed what you NACK'd.
2. **Audit the delta since your last review (per REVIEWER-SYNC.md: `git log {last_reviewed_commit}..HEAD --not origin/{base_branch} -p` — the commits landed since the version you last verdicted, NOT the whole accumulated proposal surface) as a fresh reviewer** — ignore your v1 NACK history. Read that diff as if you'd never seen the prior version. Apply your lens (security threat-model, concurrency races, contract AC, line-by-line bugs, silent-fallback shapes — whichever your role owns) to the delta itself, not to whether your previous concerns were satisfied. **Mandate 2 is bounded to this delta** — it does NOT ask you to re-traverse the whole accumulated surface from earlier cycles; that work was amortized when you first reviewed those commits.

Both mandates have equal weight. If (1) passes but (2) finds new issues, you NACK. ACK requires both pass.

**The named-blockers anchor is a known trap. Every reviewer lens has a mandate-2 in its own territory** — security has newly-introduced threat surfaces, concurrency has newly-introduced races, contract has newly-introduced AC drift, code has newly-introduced line-by-line bugs. The four issues that escaped PR #2724 to the GitHub bot were all of code-lens shape (`${ANSWER}` as bare Python, deprecated `datetime.utcnow()`, non-atomic write, bare `except: pass`) — the persistent reviewer correctly answered mandate 1 ("did prior issues get fixed? yes") and skipped mandate 2 ("does this delta introduce new issues? actually yes"). The shape generalizes: whatever your lens, this delta can introduce issues your prior NACK didn't name. Watching the producer deliver a targeted fix pulls strongly toward "verify my fix-request landed → ACK." Recognize the pull and do mandate 2 anyway.

**How to execute mandate 2:**

- Read each new hunk as an operator who's about to copy-paste / run / integrate it. Would this code execute as written? Would these docs send a copy-paster down a working path?
- Apply every rubric pass to the new hunks. New issues outside the scope of your prior NACK are blocking; your prior NACK does not bound this re-review.
- **Fresh-reviewer simulation.** Before issuing your v2 verdict, ask: would a reviewer who has only seen this delta (the commits since your last review) with no NACK history ACK this? If you can't argue yes from that diff alone, NACK.
- **External-bot anchor.** Imagine `egg-reviewer[bot]` reads only this delta (the commits since your last review) with no NACK context. What would it flag? Anything it'd flag, you should NACK first.

**Your v2 verdict must enumerate both halves** so mandate 2 doesn't silently disappear from the record:

- (a) Which v1 blockers you verified-fixed (mandate 1).
- (b) What new issues you audited-and-did-not-find (mandate 2). Name the specific shapes you checked — not "reviewed thoroughly," but "checked for silent fallbacks, doc-snippet executability, API-deprecation, atomicity of file writes." If you can't enumerate (b), you haven't done mandate 2.

**Re-reviews are cheap by design.** Your amortized context means the work is "read the delta, apply your rubric, decide" — minutes, not hours. NACK without hesitance; the orchestrator absorbs cycles. Two NACKs on the same producer where the second names new findings is the correct trajectory, not goalpost-moving. The downstream GitHub reviewer should find nothing in this delta. Anything it catches that lives in this cycle's diff is a miss attributable to this re-review.

Reviewed `.egg-state/drafts/2817-plan.md` (2401 lines) end-to-end. The plan adopts the architect's v2 28-slice DAG verbatim, enumerates per-slice tasks with role assignments and acceptance criteria, and addresses all 5 risk_analyst blockers (blocker-1..5). Most of the plan is high quality. Two slices have a concrete invocation-path bug that will break the program post-merge — these are hard NACKs because they affect the canonical CLI (`egg-orch`) and the sandbox container build/boot.

### Primitive-existence audit (verified)

| primitive | citation in plan | verification | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PipelineToolHandler` class | mcp_tools.py:1117 | `grep -n '^class PipelineToolHandler' orchestrator/mcp_tools.py` | `1117:class PipelineToolHandler:` ✓ |
| `GatewayClient` class | gateway_client.py:410 | `grep -n '^class GatewayClient' orchestrator/gateway_client.py` | `410:class GatewayClient:` ✓ |
| `KubernetesSpawner` class | kubernetes_spawner.py:321 | grep | `321:class KubernetesSpawner:` ✓ |
| `WorktreeManager` class | worktree_manager.py:140 | grep | `140:class WorktreeManager:` ✓ |
| `PeerConsensusTracker` class | peer_consensus.py:69 | grep | `69:class PeerConsensusTracker:` ✓ |
| `CheckpointHandler` class | checkpoint_handler.py:376 | grep | `376:class CheckpointHandler:` ✓ |
| `OverseerMonitor` class | monitor.py:82 | grep | `82:class OverseerMonitor:` ✓ |
| `phases_bp` blueprint | phases.py:52 (implied) | `grep -n '^phases_bp = '` | `52:phases_bp = Blueprint("phases", ...)` ✓ |
| `signals_bp` blueprint | signals.py:166 (implied) | grep | `166:signals_bp = Blueprint("signals", ...)` ✓ |
| `deployment_bp` blueprint | deployment.py:59 (implied) | grep | `59:deployment_bp = Blueprint("deployment", ...)` ✓ |
| 8 lazy `from routes.pipelines` in phases.py | lines 405,535,612,711,733,1010,1189,1307 | grep | all 8 lines confirmed ✓ |
| 2 lazy `from orchestrator.routes.pipelines` in mcp_tools.py | lines 1609,1680 | grep | `1609:_read_phase_draft, 1680:_pipeline_identifier` ✓ |
| Pattern doc `#2261` references at lines 5,26,261,276,308 (TASK-1-2) | per plan | `grep -n '#2261' docs/guides/decomposition-pattern.md` | exactly those 5 lines ✓ |
| `orchestrator/CLAUDE.md` 11× `#2261` (TASK-1-2) | per plan | `grep -c '#2261'` | 11 matches ✓ |
| `gateway/CLAUDE.md` 8× `#2261` (TASK-1-2) | per plan | `grep -c '#2261'` | 8 matches ✓ |
| `validate_forest` at plan_parser.py | TASK-25-1 | `grep -n '^def validate_forest'` | `1480:def validate_forest(...)` ✓ |

### Blocking

**1. TASK-13-1 — sandbox/egg_lib/orch_cli.py decomposition silently breaks `egg-orch` CLI invocation.**

The plan describes TASK-13-1 as "Step-0 baseline: `git mv sandbox/egg_lib/orch_cli.py sandbox/egg_lib/orch_cli/__init__.py`. Verify the `egg-orch` console-script entry point in pyproject.toml / setup.cfg still resolves to the package. `make test-all` green." and the acceptance is "`egg-orch --help` runs without error".

This rests on a false primitive assumption. `egg-orch` is **NOT** a console-script entry in any pyproject.toml — I verified `pyproject.toml`, `sandbox/pyproject.toml`, `shared/egg_contracts/pyproject.toml`, `shared/pyproject.toml`. `pyproject.toml:47-52` explicitly notes that the top-level egg CLI was removed in #1762 and only `bin/egg-deploy`, `bin/egg-sdlc`, `bin/egg-status` shell scripts remain.

`egg-orch` is instead a **symlink**: `ls -la sandbox/bin/egg-orch` returns `egg-orch -> ../egg_lib/orch_cli.py` and `readlink` confirms `../egg_lib/orch_cli.py`. The file the symlink points to is the 4034-LOC `orch_cli.py` itself (verified `wc -l sandbox/bin/egg-orch sandbox/egg_lib/orch_cli.py` → both 4034 lines via symlink resolution). Running `egg-orch …` executes the symlink target via its `#!/usr/bin/env python3` shebang.

After TASK-13-1's `git mv sandbox/egg_lib/orch_cli.py sandbox/egg_lib/orch_cli/__init__.py`:
- `sandbox/egg_lib/orch_cli.py` no longer exists at that path.
- `sandbox/bin/egg-orch -> ../egg_lib/orch_cli.py` dangles.
- The kernel cannot resolve the symlink → `egg-orch --help` fails with `No such file or directory`.
- Worse, this is the canonical CLI the entire BRC protocol relies on (this very review uses `egg-orch consensus ack` / `egg-orch message wait-loop` etc.).

The "verify console-script entry … still resolves" acceptance criterion is doubly misleading: (a) there is no console-script entry; (b) the symlink test, if run via the bare path, would fail post-mv. The producer would notice on `make test-all` (because `sandbox/tests/test_brc_cli_args.py` imports `from egg_lib.orch_cli import …` which would still resolve via the new sub-package), but the **CLI invocation surface** isn't exercised by tests — so a green test suite would hide the broken `egg-orch` invocation.

**Fix**: Add a TASK-13-N that (a) creates `sandbox/egg_lib/orch_cli/__main__.py` with the CLI dispatch logic (the `if __name__ == "__main__": main()` shape), mirroring the worked reference `scripts/select_tests/__main__.py:34 LOC` and (b) updates the `sandbox/bin/egg-orch` symlink to point to `../egg_lib/orch_cli/__main__.py` (or replaces the symlink with a shell wrapper invoking `python -m egg_lib.orch_cli "$@"`). Acceptance should include: `egg-orch --help` runs from a freshly-checked-out slice-13 branch without error; the symlink resolves; `make test-all` green.

The same concern likely does **not** apply to `egg-checkpoint` because `sandbox/bin/egg-checkpoint -> ../egg_lib/checkpoint_cli.py` is a different file — `sandbox/egg_lib/checkpoint_cli.py` is a 1062-byte WRAPPER that does `from egg_contracts.checkpoint_cli import …`. After slice-25 decomposes `shared/egg_contracts/checkpoint_cli.py` into a sub-package, the import resolves through the barrel `__init__.py`. So slice-17 / slice-25 are unaffected. The bug is specific to slice-13 because `sandbox/egg_lib/orch_cli.py` IS the 4034-LOC implementation, not a wrapper.

**2. TASK-19-1 — sandbox/entrypoint.py decomposition breaks the sandbox container Dockerfile build.**

The plan describes TASK-19-1 as "Step-0 baseline: `git mv sandbox/entrypoint.py sandbox/entrypoint/__init__.py`. Verify the in-pod entrypoint invocation (CMD/ENTRYPOINT in sandbox/Dockerfile) still resolves. `make test-all` green." and the acceptance is "`python -m sandbox.entrypoint --help` (or equivalent invocation) succeeds".

The acceptance hedge "or equivalent invocation" is too vague to catch the actual failure mode. Verified the Dockerfile invocation pattern:

```
sandbox/Dockerfile:322: COPY sandbox/entrypoint.py /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.py
sandbox/Dockerfile:323: RUN chmod +x /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.py
sandbox/Dockerfile:327: ENTRYPOINT ["python3", "/usr/local/bin/entrypoint.py"]
```

After TASK-19-1's `git mv sandbox/entrypoint.py sandbox/entrypoint/__init__.py`:
- `sandbox/entrypoint.py` no longer exists at that path.
- The Dockerfile's `COPY sandbox/entrypoint.py /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.py` **fails at image build time** with "file not found".
- Even if the COPY were updated to `COPY sandbox/entrypoint/ /usr/local/bin/entrypoint/`, `ENTRYPOINT ["python3", "/usr/local/bin/entrypoint.py"]` still points at a nonexistent file.
- Even if both lines are updated, `python3 /usr/local/bin/entrypoint/__init__.py` directly invokes `__init__.py` which won't correctly resolve relative imports (`from ._config import …`) unless invoked as a module (`python -m entrypoint`).

`make test-all` will NOT catch this because the Dockerfile build is not exercised by the in-cluster Python test runner — only `make build` or the deployment pipeline does. The first time this breaks is when an agent pod tries to start in production.

**Fix**: Update TASK-19-1's files list to include `sandbox/Dockerfile`, and add explicit acceptance criteria:
- (a) Add `sandbox/entrypoint/__main__.py` with the CLI shim (`if __name__ == "__main__": main()` invoking the cluster-extracted entrypoint logic).
- (b) Update `sandbox/Dockerfile:322` to `COPY sandbox/entrypoint/ /usr/local/bin/entrypoint/`.
- (c) Update `sandbox/Dockerfile:327` to `ENTRYPOINT ["python3", "-m", "entrypoint"]` (with `WORKDIR /usr/local/bin` set earlier, or use `python3 /usr/local/bin/entrypoint/__main__.py`).
- (d) Acceptance: `docker build -f sandbox/Dockerfile .` succeeds; `docker run --rm <image> --help` runs (or the closest non-build smoke test, e.g. spinning up the container in a local k3s test).

This is the architect's td-8 invariant ("file is loaded at orchestrator boot; ImportError would brick the pipeline") applied to a different boot path — the orchestrator-pod boot in slice-2 vs the agent-pod boot in slice-19.

### Non-blocking

- **TASK-13-1's docstring claim is factually wrong**: "console-script entry point in pyproject.toml / setup.cfg" — no such entry exists. After fixing the symlink (above), retract that wording and replace with "symlink at `sandbox/bin/egg-orch`".

- **TASK-22-2's "post-step-0 baseline" wording is wrong**: slice-22 has no step-0 commit (the `git mv` happens in slice-23 TASK-23-1). The slice-22 baseline is slice-1 HEAD plus whatever monitor.py looks like at that point. Acceptance should say "vs. slice-1 HEAD baseline" or "vs. monitor.py at the slice-22 branch base".

- **TASK-28-3's "THIS IS THE FINAL ENTRY" claim is order-dependent**: With slices 13-28 as parallel siblings of slice-1 (forest-valid, concurrency cap 2), the merge order isn't deterministic — whichever slice happens to land last drops the final entry, not necessarily slice-28. Reword the acceptance to "Drop deployment.py entry; if this is the last allowlist entry, `files:` map is empty and #2817 can close". The closing criterion is metric-based (allowlist empty), not slice-specific.

- **TASK-22-1's "≥4 seams identified" is arbitrary**: The actual constraint is "enough seams that no resulting helper exceeds 300 LOC". An implementing producer might find 3 seams that satisfy this (e.g., if the 885-LOC method has very clean natural sections of ~280 LOC each). Acceptance should be "no helper exceeds 300 LOC; PR description names the chosen seams", not a numeric ≥4 floor.

- **TASK-27-1's lazy-import preservation check via `grep -n 'from routes.pipelines'`**: The grep alone doesn't distinguish module-top vs in-function imports. Recommend strengthening to "for each grep hit, manually verify (visually in the PR diff) that the line is indented inside a function body, not at column 0". Alternatively, use an AST-walk script.

- **slice-2 multi-cluster bundle (5 cluster extractions in TASK-2-3)**: I flagged this in v1 architect review as defensible but heavy. The plan's "Chunk the PR's commit log so each extraction is its own commit" guidance partially mitigates. ACKable but watch the BRC cycle count — if slice-2 reaches >2 cycles, consider splitting.

- **slice-15 (mcp_tools.py) race with slice-2 (pipelines.py)**: TASK-15-1 notes "verify these lazy imports still resolve through pipelines' barrel after slice-2". Both slices are siblings of slice-1, so they may land in either order. Since the lazy imports are in-function (deferred to call time), either ordering works — but the note in TASK-15-1 could be stronger: "If slice-2 hasn't landed yet, the imports resolve to the unchanged pipelines.py file; if slice-2 has landed, they resolve through the new barrel — both work because lazy imports defer resolution to first invocation".

### Verdict
NACK — two blocking invocation-path bugs in slice-13 (`egg-orch` symlink dangles after `git mv`) and slice-19 (Dockerfile COPY/ENTRYPOINT references the moved `sandbox/entrypoint.py`). Both must be addressed before the program can land cleanly. Fix concretely: add `__main__.py` to the new sub-package + update the symlink (slice-13) / update the Dockerfile (slice-19) with corresponding acceptance criteria that actually exercise the invocation path. The rest of the plan is well-structured and ACK-able after these fixes.

subject: Re-review required: task_planner submitted new proposal v2
body:
Producer task_planner has submitted a new proposal (version 2) after withdrawal. Your previous confirmation was on an earlier version. Please re-review and ACK/NACK the new proposal.

**Adversarial re-review**

**Your v2 review has TWO equal-weight mandates:**

1. **Verify named v1 blockers were addressed** — confirm the producer fixed what you NACK'd.
2. **Audit the delta since your last review (`git log 7cd34bba7..f07b9a66f --not origin/<base> -p` — the commits landed since the version you last verdicted) as a fresh reviewer** — ignore your v1 NACK history. Read that diff as if you'd never seen the prior version. Apply your lens (security threat-model, concurrency races, contract AC, line-by-line bugs, silent-fallback shapes — whichever your role owns) to the delta itself, not to whether your previous concerns were satisfied. **Mandate 2 is bounded to this delta** — it does NOT ask you to re-traverse the whole accumulated surface from earlier cycles; that work was amortized when you first reviewed those commits.

Both mandates have equal weight. If (1) passes but (2) finds new issues, you NACK. ACK requires both pass.

**The named-blockers anchor is a known trap. Every reviewer lens has a mandate-2 in its own territory** — security has newly-introduced threat surfaces, concurrency has newly-introduced races, contract has newly-introduced AC drift, code has newly-introduced line-by-line bugs. The four issues that escaped PR #2724 to the GitHub bot were all of code-lens shape (`${ANSWER}` as bare Python, deprecated `datetime.utcnow()`, non-atomic write, bare `except: pass`) — the persistent reviewer correctly answered mandate 1 ("did prior issues get fixed? yes") and skipped mandate 2 ("does this delta introduce new issues? actually yes"). The shape generalizes: whatever your lens, this delta can introduce issues your prior NACK didn't name. Watching the producer deliver a targeted fix pulls strongly toward "verify my fix-request landed → ACK." Recognize the pull and do mandate 2 anyway.

**How to execute mandate 2:**

- Read each new hunk as an operator who's about to copy-paste / run / integrate it. Would this code execute as written? Would these docs send a copy-paster down a working path?
- Apply every rubric pass to the new hunks. New issues outside the scope of your prior NACK are blocking; your prior NACK does not bound this re-review.
- **Fresh-reviewer simulation.** Before issuing your v2 verdict, ask: would a reviewer who has only seen this delta (`7cd34bba7..f07b9a66f`) with no NACK history ACK this? If you can't argue yes from that diff alone, NACK.
- **External-bot anchor.** Imagine `egg-reviewer[bot]` reads only this delta (`7cd34bba7..f07b9a66f`) with no NACK context. What would it flag? Anything it'd flag, you should NACK first.

**Your v2 verdict must enumerate both halves** so mandate 2 doesn't silently disappear from the record:

- (a) Which v1 blockers you verified-fixed (mandate 1).
- (b) What new issues you audited-and-did-not-find (mandate 2). Name the specific shapes you checked — not "reviewed thoroughly," but "checked for silent fallbacks, doc-snippet executability, API-deprecation, atomicity of file writes." If you can't enumerate (b), you haven't done mandate 2.

**Re-reviews are cheap by design.** Your amortized context means the work is "read the delta, apply your rubric, decide" — minutes, not hours. NACK without hesitance; the orchestrator absorbs cycles. Two NACKs on the same producer where the second names new findings is the correct trajectory, not goalpost-moving. The downstream GitHub reviewer should find nothing in this delta. Anything it catches that lives in this cycle's diff is a miss attributable to this re-review.
